summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would create a new legal framework for stopping pests and diseases from reaching Australia and for limiting the harm they can cause.
It sets up a watchdog role, the Inspector-General of Biosecurity, to independently check how biosecurity officials do their jobs.
That watchdog would not look at the work of the Director of Human Biosecurity or the officers who handle human health risks.
changes: The bill establishes a modern regulatory framework for managing biosecurity risks, including listed human diseases, ballast water, and emergencies.
It creates the statutory position of Inspector-General of Biosecurity to review the performance and powers of biosecurity officials.
It excludes the Director of Human Biosecurity and Human Biosecurity Officers from those reviews.
summary.affected: The Australian Government, biosecurity officials, and stakeholders in Australia's biosecurity system are affected.

speeches.speaker: Barnaby Joyce
speeches.brief: Introduced the Biosecurity Bill 2014, a roughly 650-page replacement for the century-old Quarantine Act, which has been amended 50 times over 106 years, noting the Department of Agriculture cleared 16 million arriving international passengers and 26 million air cargo consignments in 2012-13, and cited ABARES modelling that a major foot-and-mouth disease outbreak could cost more than $50 billion over 10 years.

speeches.speaker: Barnaby Joyce
speeches.brief: Introduced the Biosecurity (Consequential Amendments and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2014, explaining it will make minor amendments to more than 20 pieces of Commonwealth legislation and repeal the Quarantine Act and the Quarantine Charges (Collection) Act 2014 to ensure a smooth transition to the new Biosecurity Act.

speeches.speaker: Barnaby Joyce
speeches.brief: Introduced the Quarantine Charges (Imposition-General) Amendment Bill 2014, the first of three charging bills supporting the Biosecurity Bill package, explaining it continues current cost-recovery arrangements for biosecurity activities such as scientific analysis, inspections and surveillance without setting specific charge amounts.

speeches.speaker: Alannah MacTiernan
speeches.brief: Supported the Biosecurity Bill but criticised the removal of an independent statutory Inspector-General of Biosecurity, and detailed the Department of Agriculture's investigation into Western Australian biotech company Serana, which employed 16 people with $20 million turnover and consistent compliance scores between 93 and 97 per cent, at a cost of about $235,000 including $220,000 in legal fees, before the company closed.

speeches.speaker: Angus Taylor
speeches.brief: Supported the Biosecurity Bill, said over 440 organisations were consulted over six years in developing it, cited the West African Ebola outbreak's 9,000 cases and 4,500 deaths by October as a reminder of biosecurity risks, and said improved measures could double cherry exports from 25 per cent to 50 per cent of national production.

speeches.speaker: Keith Pitt
speeches.brief: Argued that the Biosecurity Bill 2014 would modernise Australia's biosecurity system, balance trade obligations with protection for producers, and provide science-based powers to manage pests, diseases and cross-border risks, including new control orders, zones and enforcement options.

speeches.speaker: Justine Elliot
speeches.brief: Supported the Biosecurity Bill 2014 and associated quarantine bills as a modern framework for managing biosecurity risks, while urging reconsideration of ministerial control replacing an independent Inspector-General and criticising delays, funding reductions and the absence of an agricultural white paper.

speeches.speaker: Don Randall
speeches.brief: Supported the Biosecurity Bill 2014 as a modern replacement for the Quarantine Act, arguing that it would protect agriculture, public health and Australia's export reputation, simplify administration, improve compliance, reduce duplication and provide proportionate powers and penalties for managing biosecurity risks.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: Warned that replacing quarantine with risk management could weaken prevention, while supporting stronger consideration of regional differences and arguing that Australia's disease-free status, food reputation, agricultural production and export opportunities require vigilant border protection.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Scott
speeches.brief: Supported the Biosecurity Bill 2014 as a replacement for outdated quarantine legislation, using examples of pests and disease outbreaks to argue for stronger protection of agriculture, food security, wildlife and regional industries, including through emergency powers and controls on ballast water.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: Supported the Biosecurity Bill 2014 and accompanying bills, arguing that clearer legislation, emergency powers, movement restrictions and controls on ballast water would protect Australia's clean food reputation and prevent harmful pests and diseases from spreading.

speeches.speaker: Dan Tehan
speeches.brief: Supported the Biosecurity Bill 2014 as a consolidated, consultative and less burdensome framework that would protect Australia's agricultural exports and prevent serious disease incursions, while improving import risk analysis, recognising regional differences and delivering a deregulatory benefit.

speeches.speaker: Nickolas Varvaris
speeches.brief: Backed the Biosecurity Bill replacing the century-old Quarantine Act, citing Department of Agriculture figures that it cleared about 186 million international mail items and 16 million passenger arrivals in the 2013 financial year, and said invasive alien species cost Australia about $8 billion a year against a $60 billion agricultural export market.

speeches.speaker: Tony Pasin
speeches.brief: Backed the Biosecurity Bill as vital to his South Australian electorate's wine, citrus, potato, rock lobster, nut, cattle and sheep industries, updating a legislative framework designed more than a century ago.

speeches.speaker: John Cobb
speeches.brief: Backed the Biosecurity Bill, noting about two-thirds of Australia's agricultural production is exported and the century-old Quarantine Act has been amended more than 50 times, and cited AQIS finding trash on about 17 loads of imported New Zealand apples as evidence of the need for vigilant inspection.

speeches.speaker: Mark Coulton
speeches.brief: Backed the five-bill Biosecurity package, replacing an Act amended more than 50 times since 1908, warned that foot-and-mouth disease reaching Australia's uncontrollable feral pig population would devastate livestock farming, and described a Condobolin fertiliser shipment from China discovered to contain soil rather than fertiliser.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: Summed up the Biosecurity Bill debate, noting the Quarantine Act has been amended more than 50 times over 106 years and Australia's agricultural production was worth $53 billion in 2013 to 2014, and assured the House the Inspector-General of Biosecurity position and its funding, currently held by Dr Michael Bond, will continue.

speeches.speaker: Barnaby Joyce
speeches.brief: The amendment enshrines the Inspector-General of Biosecurity as a statutory position to ensure independent reviews and transparency, updating Australia’s biosecurity legislation for the first time in over 100 years and replacing the Quarantine Act 1908.
